subject: physics
title: Waves Adventure 3: Standing waves and resonance
welcome_lead: Today you'll set up standing waves on a string — and resonate.
meta_desc: Physics — standing waves, nodes and antinodes, harmonics, open/closed pipes, resonance.
final_note: You learned standing waves form from two oppositely travelling waves; harmonics: λ_n = 2L/n for fixed string; resonance amplifies at natural frequencies.

concepts.def: Vibrations perpendicular (light) or parallel (sound) to travel.
Number of waves per second and the length of one wave.
v = f × λ, the speed a wave travels.
Maximum displacement from the rest position; relates to energy.
Radio to gamma; all travel at the speed of light in a vacuum.
Waves bounce off surfaces or change direction when changing medium.

walkthroughs.body_html:
String fixed at both ends — nodes at ends.

Fundamental: λ₁ = 2L, f₁ = v/(2L).

nth harmonic: λ_n = 2L/n, f_n = nv/(2L).

Wave speed on string: v = √(T/μ), where T = tension, μ = mass/length.

Both ends open: antinodes at ends.
f_n = nv/(2L), n = 1, 2, 3,.

One closed end: node at closed, antinode at open.
f_n = nv/(4L), n = 1, 3, 5,. (odd harmonics only).

Explains why a closed pipe an octave lower than open of same L.

System has natural frequency f_0. Driving at f_0 → amplitude grows large — resonance.

- Pushing a swing in sync.
- Tacoma Narrows Bridge collapse 1940 (resonance from wind).
- MRI machines: nuclear magnetic resonance.

Damping reduces resonance peak.

mcqs.q: Which of the following is a fundamental particle: proton, electron, or neutron?
options: Only the electron — protons and neutrons are made of quarks.
All three (proton, electron, neutron) are fundamental particles that cannot be broken down.
Only the total mass in kilograms needs to balance.
Only the proton is fundamental; electrons and neutrons are composite.

mcqs.q: What is the difference between nuclear fission and fusion?
options: Only the total mass in kilograms needs to balance.
Fission and fusion are the same process, just at different scales.
Fission splits a heavy nucleus into smaller ones; fusion joins light nuclei into a heavier one.
Fission combines small atoms into bigger ones, and fusion splits them.
